Modes and Controls

You open Perplexity and start typing. The answers come back fine — usable, quick, good enough. Three searches later, you realize you've been running everything on default, and the results could have been sharper the whole time.

So, how do you make your searches deeper and more precise? In this lesson, you'll learn how to customize Perplexity with plans and modes to get exactly the results you need.
Scenario: Researching a Team Offsite
You're building the research case for a company off-site from the previous lesson. You need to:

• Get a quick overview of city options
  • Compare costs and logistics in detail
  • Find credible data to justify the budget
  • Revisit earlier research as new questions come up

feedbackCorrect.text: Default settings work for general questions — but when the task needs depth, verification, or specific source types, the right mode makes a real difference.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The issue isn't speed, volume, or readability, but how it's fitting. The same settings applied to very different questions will work well for some and fall short for others.

blocks.text: The same default settings applied to four very different tasks will fall short on at least some of them. That's what different plans solve. Let's go through it!
Plans — What's Available
Perplexity runs on three tiers:

• The free plan gives you practically unlimited standard searches for research tasks.
  • Pro unlocks access to the latest AI models trained for higher accuracy for personal use.
  • Max goes further with unlimited usage and the most advanced AI reasoning models for heavy users.
There are also two specialized plans for specific contexts.

• Education Pro for students and educators: suited for academic research and complex reports at a steep discount.
  • Business for teams that need more than personal research: premium source citations from PitchBook and Statista, compliance certifications, SSO, and data privacy guarantees.

Plans control your access level. Modes control how Perplexity thinks about your query: how deeply it reasons, which models it uses, and how it structures its answer. The results are sourced, synthesized, and ready to use regardless of which mode you're in.
Best Mode

Best is the default mode — it picks the right model for your query automatically, whether that's a quick fact-check or a deep multi-source comparison. On the free plan, Best runs silently in the background with no model selector visible. On Pro or Max, you'll see a Model dropdown where you can pick a specific model or stick with Best and let Perplexity decide.

feedbackCorrect.text: Best mode is exactly right here. You're orienting, not deciding — a fast, broad answer is what moves you forward at this stage.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Depth comes later, once you know what you're actually comparing. Best mode is the right starting point before you know which direction to go.

blocks.text: Filtering by Source Type

So, you know that modes control how Perplexity thinks about your question. Source filters control where it looks, restricting results to a specific type before the search runs. All of them are available on the free plan, and you'll find them at the top of the screen when you start a new chat.
Filters narrow the search space for Perplexity. Here's what each one does:

• Discover: Surfaces trending topics and news from across the web — good for staying current without a specific question in mind.
  • Finance: Pulls from official company financial disclosures and market data.
  • Health: Focused on medical sources, clinical data, and health publications.
  • Academic: Filters for scholarly papers and peer-reviewed journals.
  • Patents: Searches patent databases and intellectual property filings.

The best way to understand source filters is to see them in action. Imagine you need to check the US market before making any financial decisions for the trip. Instead of scrolling through news sites, you switch to Finance — and Perplexity pulls directly from market data and financial filings.
Perplexity Computer

Source filters narrow where Perplexity looks. But what if the task itself is too complex for a single search and require multiple steps, tools, and decisions along the way? Search Operators & Filters

A well-structured prompt gets you closer to what you need — but not always all the way there. Sometimes the results come back from the wrong sources, in the wrong format, or from three years ago. Search operators are how you close that gap: short commands that tell Perplexity exactly where to look, what type of content to surface, and how recent it needs to be.
What Are Search Operators
Search operators are short commands you add directly to your search. They control where Perplexity looks and what it surfaces. Think of them as filters you apply before the search runs.

Without operators, Perplexity decides which sources to pull from. With them, you decide. A personal question works fine without operators, but the moment source type, recency, or precision matters, operators close that gap.

feedbackCorrect.text: Operators earn their place when the source, format, or recency of results matters. A competitive analysis needs credible, current data in a usable format — that's exactly when operators add value.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Recent reviews might marginally improve a coffee shop recommendation — but a date filter on a casual local search would limit useful results without meaningfully improving them. Operators are for when precision matters, not for general exploration.

blocks.question: Which type of search benefits most from using a search operator?

blocks.text:
Now imagine the same search principle applied to something where the source matters — like finding current pricing data or an industry report. For that, a standard search isn't enough.

That's where operators come in. There are four worth knowing, each one solving a different problem.
Here's what each operator does:

• Site filters ("site:") restrict results to a specific domain.
  • Filetype filters ("filetype:") surface a specific document type, such as PDF or DOC.
  • Date filters ("after:"/"before:") force results within a specific time window.
  • Quotes match an exact phrase rather than individual words.
Restricting by Source

Let's start with "site:" — the operator that controls where Perplexity looks. Add it to any search, and Perplexity pulls only from that domain — no competing pages, no off-topic results. Use it when the source matters as much as the answer. See how that looks like on a simple personal question first.

blocks.prompt: You want to learn about home pruning techniques, but only from a trusted gardening institution.
blocks.template: How to prune roses [site operator]

feedbackCorrect.text: "site:" is a pre-search filter — it sets the boundaries before Perplexity starts looking. Everything outside that domain is excluded from the start, which is why the results changed completely.

feedbackIncorrect.text: "site:" doesn't interpret the question or filter results afterward. It restricts the eligible source pool before the search runs. Perplexity never considers pages outside that domain. Technical framing and post-search filtering are both separate mechanisms that have nothing to do with the site.

options.label: It signalled the question was technical, prompting Perplexity to prioritise more authoritative sources
It told Perplexity where to look before the search ran, so only that domain's content was eligible
It filtered the results after the search ran, removing lower-quality sources

blocks.question: What did the "site:" operator do?

blocks.text: That's how the source operator works! Note that it returned 10 sources only from the specific site you requested.

The same operator works just as well for professional research. Restricting to a trusted publication means credible, relevant sources appear from the start. 

Now let's look at the next operator, which controls the type of document that comes back.
Finding Specific Document Types

Some information only exists inside documents — research reports, whitepapers, official papers — not on web pages. If what you need is in a PDF or a Word file rather than an article, web results won't get you there. That's what "filetype:" solves. Add "filetype:pdf" or "filetype:doc" to any search, and Perplexity surfaces the documents directly — the reports and research papers that web pages only ever summarize. Let's say you need to find research on sleep patterns.

blocks.exampleResponse: Sleep patterns research, particularly from PDF studies, reveals key insights into how sleep cycles, durations, and disruptions affect health, cognition, and daily performance. Core Sleep Architecture Human sleep cycles through non-REM (N1-N3) and REM stages roughly 4-6 times nightly, with each cycle lasting 90-110 minutes (1955: Aserinsky/Kleitman REM discovery); early cycles emphasize deep N3 slow-wave sleep, while later ones increase REM for memory processing. Research Priorities It prioritizes biomarkers for sleep quality, chronotherapeutics for chronic conditions, and tools for early detection in youth to prevent lifelong issues (1997 NHLBI influences). Population studies highlight 30-40% of U.S. adults facing sleep deficiency, costing $411 billion yearly in health and productivity losses. Source: Sleepresearchsociety.com, Sciencedirect.com

blocks.template: Sleep patterns research [filetype operator]

blocks.text:
"filetype:pdf" went straight to the source documents where the actual data lives. Perplexity also lets you download research papers from the search results. 

But sometimes Perplexity returns data more than 10 years old, and in a fast-moving research field, that's a problem. When the data needs to be current, you need to control the time window. That's what the next operator is for.
Filtering by Date

Date filters control exactly which time range your results come from. Add "after:" or "before:" to any search, and Perplexity only returns results inside that window — everything outside it is excluded before the search runs. Use them whenever an old source would actively mislead rather than inform: pricing data, market reports, product releases, regulatory updates. Let's apply one now.

blocks.exampleResponse: Recent sleep patterns research since January 2025 has advanced understanding of chronotypes, trends in disturbances, and health links using large datasets. Chronotype Subtypes A February 2026 McGill study in Nature Communications identified five biological chronotype subtypes within night owls (3) and early birds (2), using AI on 27K+ UK Biobank adults' brain imaging, questionnaires, and records; subtypes link to unique risks like depression, cardiovascular issues, or cognitive strengths beyond simple bedtimes. These reflect genetic-lifestyle interactions, urging personalized sleep support over binary labels. Rising Sleep Issues A September 2025 Danish study (Science Advances) tracked 15-45-year-olds (2010-2021), finding self-reported sleep problems rose from 34% to 49%, with melatonin prescriptions surging 10-fold; machine learning on 2.2M life-course records clustered patterns tying sleep to pain, mental health, or early adversity. SLEEP 2025 featured Miller School posters on sleep's Alzheimer's role via Fitbit-tracked stages and biomarkers, plus discrimination-insomnia links are stronger in females. Sources: McGill.com, ScienceDirect.com, SleepResearchSociety.org

feedbackIncorrect.text: Date filter doesn't prioritize or signal anything — it excludes results outside of the range. Result quality is determined by the topic and operators combined, not by the date filter alone.

Now there's one more precision tool worth knowing — for when the words are right, but the context needs to be more exact.
Exact Phrase Matching

Putting a phrase in quotes tells Perplexity to match those words exactly in that order. With quotes, a search for "machine learning algorithm list" returns only results where that exact phrase appears. Let's say you need to find Apple's financial reports specifically. That's the kind of search where quotes make the difference.

Source: Apple.com

Each operator solves one problem, but combined, they close all the gaps at once — source, format, recency, and precision in a single search. Let's add everything together.

Operating Cash Flow: Nearly $54 billion, enabling $32 billion returned to shareholders. This PDF includes detailed statements of operations, cash flows, and balance sheets, accessible via Apple's investor relations section. No other major "Financial Reports" developments (e.g., Q2) appear post-January in PDF format yet. Source: Apple.com

Your Research HQ

Two weeks into planning the offsite. Notes in three apps, tabs you're scared to close, and a Perplexity history you re-explain every session. There's a better way to keep it all in one place — and it's called Spaces.

By the end of this lesson, you'll know how to set up a Space, upload your own files, and query directly against them — so your research builds on itself.
What Is a Space?

A Space is a persistent project environment inside Perplexity. It keeps your research threads, uploaded files, custom instructions, and collaborators in one place, so every session picks up where the last one left off.
Without a Space, every new thread starts fresh. You carry the overhead of re-establishing context, re-uploading files, and re-explaining priorities every time. Let's try creating a Space.
Creating Your First Space
Click New Space in the right sidebar, give it a name like "Team Offsite 2026," and you're in. From here, you can add instructions, upload files, and invite collaborators.

Before you create your first Space, Perplexity shows you a selection of pre-built templates — things like Trip Planner Pro, Research Assistant, and more. Pick one that fits your task and it opens ready to use. For your offsite task, you can use the "Trip Planner Pro" template.

Templates are designed for quick, one-off use — they're not saved to your Spaces by default, and they work best as-is rather than something you'd customize or share. For a project you'll keep coming back to, there's a better move.

Templates are a starting point, not a finished workspace. To unlock the full power of Spaces — sharing, file uploads, custom instructions — copy the template's instructions and paste them into your own new Space. Everything then works the way you'd expect.

blocks.text: That's exactly what we'll do with the Trip Planner Pro template. Create a new Space called "Team Offsite 2026," and paste the instructions under Space instructions. From that point, every search in the Space runs with that framing already built in.

The custom instruction can be as detailed as you need it to be. You can set the tone, format, priorities, and constraints. 

In this case, it's set up as a travel planning assistant that asks clarifying questions, builds day-by-day itineraries, and includes local tips. Everything typed here runs silently behind every search in the Space. Let's run a search with that instruction.

Total budget: $800-1200/person (excl. flights). Use Bolt/Uber + 72h tram pass ($15). Day 1: Arrival & Kickoff — Arrive, lunch at Lokál ($15). — 3-7 p.m.: Alignment workshop + Old Town treasure hunt ($50/pp). — Dinner at U Fleků beer hall ($30). Day 2: Deep Work — 9 a.m.-1 p.m.: Strategy sessions (roadmap/SWOT). — 2-5 p.m.: Axe throwing/escape room ($30/pp). — Evening: Prague Castle stroll + dinner at Eska ($40). Turn Research Into a Workflow

You've compared cities, built a Space, flagged budget risks, and mapped out cost-saving options. The research is solid. But now you need the next crucial step — a finished plan. That's a different kind of task. And Perplexity has a different tool for it.
Perplexity Computer

Computer is a separate workspace inside Perplexity. You'll find it in the left sidebar. It's not a search mode or a research feature. It's where you hand off tasks that have multiple steps and need a finished result at the end.

Computer works through a task the way you would — it searches, reads pages, cross-references sources, uses your files, and keeps going until the deliverable is ready. The difference is it does all of that without you driving every step.

feedbackCorrect.text: Spot on! Deep Research produces a sourced report — that's its job. Computer goes further: it works through the task end-to-end and hands you something finished, like a plan, a brief, or a structured document ready to share.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The difference isn't speed, length, or model quality. It's actually what gets handed back. Deep Research returns research, and Computer returns a deliverable.

blocks.question: What makes Computer different from running a Deep Research query in Perplexity?

blocks.text: What Computer Is For
Not every task needs Computer. The right signal is this: does the task have multiple steps and a specific output at the end?
Here's how Computer fits alongside everything else:

• Search answers a single question
  • Deep Research produces a sourced research report
  • Spaces keep context, files, and threads in one place
  • Computer executes a multi-step task and delivers the finished result

feedbackCorrect.text: Right on! A single lookup doesn't need Computer. A quick search returns this in seconds. Computer is for tasks with multiple steps and a real deliverable at the end.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Computer is built for multi-step workflows. Sending a single factual question to Computer is like hiring a project manager to check one price. The tool is doing far less than it's built for.

Starting a Task in Computer
Click Computer in the sidebar, and you'll see a text input field. This is where you describe what you need. Remember that the task shouldn't be a search query, but a clear outcome with context.
Before you type, think through four things:

• What you need produced
  • What context Computer should use
  • What the constraints are
  • What the output should look like
The clearer the handoff, the better the result is suited for you.

Skills for Repeatable Workflows

Every repeated task comes with a hidden cost: rewriting the same instructions, reformatting the same output, running the same checks. Skills eliminate that. Store the process once, and Computer follows it every time you need that kind of work done.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to use Skills to your advantage. Let's go!
What Are Skills?

Skills are reusable capabilities for Perplexity Computer — step-by-step instructions it can automatically apply whenever a matching task comes up. You may have seen something similar in Claude, where Skills standardize how it writes or responds. Computer Skills go further: they're full automated workflows that Computer can re-run across models and tools, turning your instructions into a production-ready capability.
A Skill can store anything Computer needs to approach a type of task consistently:

• Structure and workflow steps
  • Tone and formatting rules
  • Review criteria and quality checks
  • Brand standards and assets
  • Output requirements
Once a Skill is set up, Computer applies it every time that kind of work comes up. You won't need to re-explain the task, context, or requirements.

feedbackCorrect.text: Nailed it! A Skill stores the method — structure, steps, review criteria — not just the task. That's what makes it reusable across every new task of the same type.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Context and source preferences are useful in a prompt, but they don't make a process repeatable. A Skill defines how Computer approaches a type of work — not just what information it starts with.

options.label: The topic and context of the task, so Computer doesn't need background information each time
A set of source preferences so Computer always pulls from the same places

blocks.text: Where to Find Skills

Open Customise in the sidebar and click the Skills tab. You'll see three views: All, My skills, and Example skills. Example Skills are pre-built templates you can use as-is or as a starting point for your own.
Each Skill has a name, a description of when to use it, and a SKILL.md file with the full instructions. Open any example to see what a complete Skill looks like before you build your own.
Creating a Skill
Click + Create skill in the top right. You'll see two options: "Create with Computer" builds the Skill through a conversation, and "Upload a skill" lets you import an existing .md or .zip file.

"Create with Computer" is the easiest starting point. Click the option, and Perplexity already has a head start — it uses its own built-in "create-skill" Skill to open the conversation. Computer asks you questions about the task, the context and intended user, and what a good result looks like. You answer, and it builds the Skill from there.
Upload a skill is useful when instructions already exist somewhere else: a process doc, a team playbook, or a Skill from another platform. Export it as a .md file or a .zip and import it directly.

feedbackCorrect.text: That's it! Computer doesn't carry memory between tasks — the Skill is what kept the output consistent. It defined the method once, and Computer applied it every time.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Computer doesn't retain formatting from previous tasks. Without a Skill, each report would start fresh — the structure only repeats because the Skill stores it explicitly.

Your AI Still Doesn't Know You

You've built a Space, handed workflows to Computer, and created Skills for repeated tasks. But every time a new task starts, you're still the one copying in the latest email, the updated budget, and the calendar conflict. Computer is capable, but it doesn't have access to where the work actually lives. That's what Connectors change.

In this lesson, you'll connect Computer to the tools you already use, learn when it can take action on your behalf, and set up a workflow that runs automatically.
What Are Connectors?

Connectors link Perplexity Computer to the apps where your work lives. Without them, Computer only knows what you paste in. With them, it can pull from your inbox, calendar, files, and project tools, and work with the current state of your work, not a snapshot you manually assembled.

Your team lead emails a new constraint for the Prague offsite. Your coordinator updates a checklist in Notion. Two people mark themselves unavailable on Friday in Google Calendar. Without Connectors, you copy all of that in yourself, but with them, Computer reads it directly and works from there!
Where to Find Connectors

Open Customise in the sidebar and click the Connectors tab. You'll see four views: Discover, All, Connected, and Available. Some connectors are included with Computer at no extra cost — others are available to add.

News & Trend Analysis

You wake up to a flood of messages about something that happened overnight — a platform changed its algorithm, a brand said something it shouldn't have, a market shifted. Everyone is reacting. You want to understand what happened.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to track breaking news, compare sources, and turn a research session into a structured report you can act on.

feedbackCorrect.text: A breaking story evolves fast. A result from this morning and a result from last week can appear side by side — and they're often describing different stages of the same event. Publication date is what tells you which version of the story you're actually reading.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Outlet reputation and source consensus both matter for credibility — but neither tells you where a result sits in the news cycle. A well-known outlet's coverage from three days ago may already be outdated, and consensus across sources can simply mean the same early report got widely picked up. Date is what orients you first.

options.label: When each result was published, since stories change fast
How many sources cover the same angle — consensus signals the information is reliable
Which outlet published it — bigger publications are more accurate on breaking news

blocks.question: You open the web to follow a breaking story. There are dozens of results from different outlets and different time periods. What's the most important thing to pay attention to?

blocks.text:
Searching for a breaking story without filters is like opening a firehose. You get opinion pieces, outdated takes, and reactions to reactions — mixed in with the actual facts. The story gets harder to understand.

Perplexity makes that easier: you can filter by date, compare perspectives, and verify claims in one place instead of switching between tabs. The first thing to add to any breaking news search is a date filter.
Tracking Breaking News

You learned how date operators work in Lesson 5. Here, they do the same job in a news context — restricting results to a specific window, whether that's the last 24 hours, last week, or last month. In a fast-moving story, that single addition keeps the results focused on today's development. Let's apply it to a news search.

blocks.exampleResponse: Instagram's algorithm in 2026 focuses more on user‑declared interests and long‑term engagement than on raw likes or follower count. Reels are now ranked heavily on watch time and skip rate, and smaller creators get a slight boost if their content is original and well‑watched. For a creator or a brand: — Prioritize original, platform‑native Reels and strong hooks. — Use fewer, more specific hashtags (3-5) to signal clear topics. — Focus on watch time, comments, shares, and profile visits rather than just posting volume. How to find the official announcement you're tracking If you're specifically looking for Instagram's own public announcement page dated after 2026‑03‑03, the most reliable sources are: — The Instagram Creators section of the Meta Newsroom and Instagram's official blog. — Meta's "Creator Updates" newsletter and Instagram's @creators account, which highlight new algorithmic tweaks and feature rollouts. Sources: TheBusinesNews, InfinityDigitalSpace

feedbackCorrect.text: The newsroom suggestion is Perplexity pointing you to where the claim originated. What follows makes the result citable, not just useful.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Current coverage tells you which outlets are reporting, not what Instagram actually said, so ignoring the suggestion leaves you working from a secondary source. And coming back later adds an unnecessary step when the primary source is already in reach — the suggestion is there because the claim needs confirming now, not eventually.

The same story reads differently depending on who's telling it. Instagram's newsroom says the change helps creators. Analysts say it disrupts brands. Creators report mixed results on the ground. None of them is wrong; they're just seeing different parts of the same thing. So let's try pulling from more than one source.

Source Credibility & Verification

A statistic lands in your presentation. It sounds authoritative. It has a citation. But the citation links to a think tank funded by the company whose product it praises.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to evaluate what you find before it ends up in something you've signed your name to.
Not All Sources Are Equal
A citation isn't the same as credibility. The question is whether the source behind the citation holds up: who published it, when, whether they had a stake in the conclusion, and how they got there.
There are four things worth checking on any source:

• Outlet credibility: Who published it and what their editorial standards are.
  • Publication date: Whether the data reflects current conditions.
  • Independence: Whether the publisher had a stake in the conclusion.
  • Methodology: Whether the research method is visible and sound.
Miss one and you might be building on something that looks solid but isn't.

feedbackCorrect.text: Funding, recency, and methodology are the three things most likely to hide problems in a statistic. A funder with a stake in the outcome can shape the study without the data being technically wrong, and recency and methodology catch what funding bias doesn't.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Wide citation means the claim spread — not that anyone verified it. A statistic repeated across 10 articles still traces back to one original source that needs checking. And major publications regularly cite research without auditing the methodology behind it — a well-known outlet name is not a substitute for checking who funded the study, when it was conducted, and how.
